cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series
cards.body: Programme 7 · Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse

cards.title: Welcome to Level 2
cards.body: This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens your ability to manage complex childhood conditions, interpret paediatric trends, calculate medicines safely, communicate across cultures and coordinate multidisciplinary care.

bullets.label: Designed for Internationally Qualified Nurses preparing for global paediatric practice and NCLEX readiness.

cards.title: What You Will Learn
cards.body: By the end of this programme, you will be equipped to deliver safe, evidence-informed paediatric care across all clinical settings.

bullets.label: Apply internationally recognised paediatric assessment tools
Prioritise care using age-specific physiological risk
Recognise and escalate paediatric deterioration promptly
Apply paediatric medication and infusion safety principles
Support children with chronic illness and developmental needs
Provide trauma-informed and culturally responsive care
Recognise concerns and follow reporting pathways

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: Age Matters

bullets.label: A normal adult value may be critically abnormal in a child. Assessment must always be age-contextualised.
A quiet child may be more concerning than a distressed one. Subtle changes demand clinical attention.
Caregiver concerns are clinically valid. "This is not my child" should always prompt immediate assessment.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Advanced Paediatric Assessment & Prioritisation

bullets.label: Prioritise care using age-specific physiological risk

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Core Assessment Frameworks

bullets.label: Rapidly evaluates appearance, breathing and circulation — a critical first-look tool before hands-on assessment.
Structured approach for urgent assessment —
bullets.text: Structured approach for urgent assessment — Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure — applied systematically in all emergency scenarios.

bullets.label: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, delayed capillary
bullets.text: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, delayed capillary refill and altered interaction must be interpreted within the child's developmental context.

bullets.label: Identify the child, age, weight, current
bullets.text: Identify the child, age, weight, current concern, relevant history, assessment findings and required action — every time.

cards.title: SECTION 1 · CLINICAL EXAMPLE
cards.body: Recognising Opioid-Related Deterioration

bullets.label: A parent reports her child is unusually sleepy
bullets.text: A parent reports her child is unusually sleepy after minor surgery. Vital signs are near expected range, but the child is difficult to rouse and breathing more slowly.

bullets.label: Clinical Action: The nurse recognises possible
bullets.text: Clinical Action: The nurse recognises possible opioid-related deterioration and escalates immediately — without waiting for vital signs to become overtly abnormal.

bullets.label: Combine tools with clinical judgement — escalate on concern, not only scoring thresholds.
Parental concern is a valid clinical finding. Never dismiss it.
A worsening trend within the normal range may be more dangerous than a single abnormal reading.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions

bullets.label: High-risk paediatric conditions can deteriorate
bullets.text: High-risk paediatric conditions can deteriorate rapidly. Nurses must anticipate complications, deliver age-appropriate interventions and coordinate care with specialist teams — before hypotension appears.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Emergency Condition Categories

bullets.label: Severe asthma, upper-airway obstruction and
bullets.text: Severe asthma, upper-airway obstruction and respiratory failure — rapid oxygenation, medication and escalation readiness.

bullets.label: Prolonged seizure, meningitis, raised ICP — airway protection, neuro-monitoring and urgent treatment initiation.
Sepsis, shock, severe dehydration — tachycardia and altered behaviour may precede hypotension significantly.
DKA and electrolyte emergencies — careful fluid, insulin and neurological monitoring per paediatric protocols.
Hypotension is a late sign in paediatric shock. Do not wait for it before activating the emergency pathway.

cards.title: SECTION 2 · CLINICAL EXAMPLE
cards.body: Recognising Paediatric Sepsis

bullets.label: A child with fever develops a non-blanching rash, prolonged capillary refill and lethargy.
The nurse recognises possible sepsis, activates
bullets.text: The nurse recognises possible sepsis, activates the emergency pathway and obtains appropriate access — without waiting for hypotension.

bullets.label: Treat airway and breathing changes urgently

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Medication Safety, Chronic Illness & Discharge

bullets.label: Children with chronic or complex conditions may
bullets.text: Children with chronic or complex conditions may rely on multiple medicines, devices and caregivers across hospital, school and community settings. Safe care requires precise calculation, thorough education and seamless coordination.

bullets.label: Recalculate doses whenever the child's weight changes.
Support — but never replace — manual verification of infusion parameters.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Chronic Conditions & Care Coordination

bullets.label: Long-term management plans that integrate education, self-management and school support.
Rescue medication plans, seizure diaries and family training are essential components of safe discharge.
Paediatricians, nurses, pharmacists,
bullets.text: Paediatricians, nurses, pharmacists, therapists, school staff and community services — responsibilities must be clearly defined.

bullets.label: Use teach-back and return demonstration to confirm family understanding before every discharge.

cards.title: SECTION 3 · CLINICAL EXAMPLE
cards.body: Epilepsy Discharge: Safe Handover in Practice

bullets.label: Structured family education reduces emergency
bullets.text: Structured family education reduces emergency re-admissions and empowers caregivers to act confidently during a seizure event at home or school.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Safeguarding, Communication & Culturally Safe Care

bullets.label: International paediatric nurses must uphold
bullets.text: International paediatric nurses must uphold children's rights, recognise safeguarding concerns and communicate in ways that respect culture, family structure and the child's developing autonomy.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Four Pillars of Safe & Rights-Respecting Care

bullets.label: An adolescent asks to speak privately about
bullets.text: An adolescent asks to speak privately about medication and home safety. The nurse explains confidentiality and its limits, listens without judgement, and follows the safeguarding pathway when immediate risk is disclosed.

bullets.label: Know local safeguarding and consent requirements
Explain confidentiality honestly and its limits

cards.body: GNPS Programme 7 · Level 2 Complete

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 7 · Paediatric Nursing

bullets.label: Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse (IQN) · Section 1: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation

cards.title: What You Will Learn
cards.body: This section equips internationally qualified nurses with the clinical frameworks and judgement skills needed to assess and prioritise care for children in a variety of settings.

bullets.label: Use ABCDE and the Paediatric Assessment Triangle in clinical practice.
Interpret findings within the correct developmental context.
Recognise subtle changes before measurements become abnormal.
Communicate deterioration clearly, promptly, and professionally.

cards.title: Why Paediatric Assessment Is Different
cards.body: Children are not small adults. They compensate physiologically until late in illness — making early, structured assessment critical for detecting deterioration before it becomes life-threatening.

bullets.label: Subtle behavioural changes and carer concerns may precede measurable clinical deterioration. Never dismiss them.

cards.title: Core Assessment Frameworks
cards.body: Two Essential Tools

bullets.label: Airway · Breathing · Circulation · Disability ·
bullets.text: Airway · Breathing · Circulation · Disability · Exposure. Supports urgent, structured assessment in any deteriorating child.

bullets.label: Rapid evaluation of Appearance, Work of Breathing, and Circulation to Skin — completed in under 30 seconds.

cards.title: Age-Specific Interpretation of Vital Signs
cards.body: Normal ranges shift significantly across childhood. Tachycardia, tachypnoea, delayed capillary refill, and altered responsiveness must always be interpreted within the child's developmental stage.

bullets.label: Using adult reference ranges in children is a
bullets.text: Using adult reference ranges in children is a common error that leads to missed deterioration. Always consult age-appropriate charts and clinical guidelines.

cards.title: Listening to Parents and Carers
cards.body: "This is not my child."

bullets.label: Parents are expert observers of their child's
bullets.text: Parents are expert observers of their child's normal behaviour. When a caregiver expresses concern — even without clear clinical evidence — this should always prompt a formal reassessment.

bullets.label: Unusual quietness, reduced interaction, or irritability may precede measurable deterioration.
Reduced intake or altered feeding behaviour can be an early warning sign in infants.
Consistent family concern is a clinical prompt — treat it with the same weight as a physiological finding.

cards.title: Recognising Deterioration: Clinical Example
cards.body: Scenario

bullets.label: A parent reports her child is unusually sleepy
bullets.text: A parent reports her child is unusually sleepy following minor surgery. Vital signs are near the expected range, but the child is difficult to rouse and breathing more slowly than before.

bullets.label: The nurse recognises possible opioid-related
bullets.text: The nurse recognises possible opioid-related respiratory depression and escalates immediately — acting on clinical concern before scoring thresholds are breached.

cards.title: Structured Escalation Communication
cards.body: When escalating concern about a deteriorating child, structured communication ensures no critical information is missed.

bullets.label: Current clinical concern — what has changed
Escalate based on clinical concern, not only when a scoring threshold is crossed.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Combine tools with judgement

bullets.label: Assessment frameworks guide — but do not replace — clinical thinking and experience.
Every finding must be considered within the child's age, development, and baseline.
Treat carer concerns as clinical data
A worried parent is a valid clinical indicator — listen carefully and act accordingly.
Act on concern, not just scores. Timely, structured escalation saves lives.

cards.title: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 7: Paediatric Nursing · Section 2

cards.title: Section 2 Overview
cards.body: Every Child Deserves Exceptional Care

bullets.label: High-risk paediatric conditions can deteriorate
bullets.text: High-risk paediatric conditions can deteriorate rapidly. Nurses must anticipate complications, deliver age-appropriate interventions, and coordinate care with specialist teams to ensure the best possible outcomes.

bullets.label: Early warning signs before deterioration occurs

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify and manage common high-risk paediatric presentations across all body systems
Identify airway, neurological and circulatory emergencies before they become life-threatening
Deliver safe, age-appropriate emergency interventions using paediatric-specific protocols
Continuously assess and document the child's response to treatment and escalate as needed

cards.title: Respiratory Emergencies
cards.body: Respiratory failure is one of the most common causes of paediatric cardiac arrest. Early recognition and intervention are critical.

bullets.label: Look for: silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion,
bullets.text: Look for: silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, SpO₂ <92%. Administer bronchodilators, systemic steroids and high-flow oxygen immediately.

bullets.label: Croup and epiglottitis present with stridor and
bullets.text: Croup and epiglottitis present with stridor and increased work of breathing. Minimise distress; prepare for escalation to anaesthetics.

bullets.label: Signs include altered consciousness, exhaustion
bullets.text: Signs include altered consciousness, exhaustion and central cyanosis. Support airway and breathing; prepare for ventilatory support.

cards.title: Neurological Emergencies
cards.body: Priority: Protect the Airway First

bullets.label: Neurological emergencies in children require
bullets.text: Neurological emergencies in children require rapid assessment using the AVPU scale and urgent intervention to prevent secondary brain injury.

bullets.label: Administer benzodiazepines per weight-based
bullets.text: Administer benzodiazepines per weight-based protocol. Protect from injury. Prepare for RSI if seizure continues beyond 30 minutes.

bullets.label: Classic triad: fever, photophobia, neck
bullets.text: Classic triad: fever, photophobia, neck stiffness. Give antibiotics without delay — do not wait for LP. Monitor for raised ICP.

bullets.label: Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia,
bullets.text: Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing. Nurse at 30°, avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia, urgent neurosurgical review.

cards.title: Circulatory & Infectious Emergencies
cards.body: Children may maintain blood pressure until they are severely compromised. Hypotension is a late and pre-terminal sign in paediatric shock.

bullets.label: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, altered
bullets.text: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, altered behaviour. Activate the sepsis pathway: cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, IV access, fluid bolus.

bullets.label: Poor perfusion, prolonged capillary refill (>2
bullets.text: Poor perfusion, prolonged capillary refill (>2 sec), mottled skin. Give 10 ml/kg isotonic fluid bolus; reassess after each bolus.

bullets.label: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes,
bullets.text: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output, altered consciousness. Fluid resuscitation guided by weight and clinical response.

bullets.label: Hypotension in a child indicates decompensated
bullets.text: Hypotension in a child indicates decompensated shock — act immediately. Do not wait for this sign before initiating treatment.

cards.title: Metabolic Emergencies
cards.body: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)

bullets.label: DKA in children carries a risk of cerebral oedema — the leading cause of DKA-related mortality in paediatrics.
Calculate fluid deficit carefully; avoid rapid rehydration
Insulin infusion commenced after initial fluid resuscitation
Hourly neurological observations — watch for headache, behaviour change
Monitor glucose, potassium and pH frequently
Severe hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia can precipitate seizures and cardiac arrhythmias.
Hyponatraemia: Correct sodium slowly — rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination
Hyperkalaemia: ECG changes indicate cardiac risk — calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, sodium bicarbonate
Always use paediatric weight-based dosing protocols

cards.title: Clinical Example: Recognising Sepsis Early
cards.body: A child presents with fever, a non-blanching rash, prolonged capillary refill and lethargy. The nurse does not wait for hypotension — sepsis is suspected immediately.

bullets.label: This case illustrates a core NCLEX principle:
bullets.text: This case illustrates a core NCLEX principle: in paediatric shock, act on early signs, not late ones. Waiting for hypotension may cost a child's life.

cards.title: Core Paediatric Assessment Principles
cards.body: Airway & Breathing First

bullets.label: Always address airway and breathing changes urgently. Children desaturate faster than adults — seconds matter.
Establish access early. Intraosseous access is acceptable if IV access fails. Fluid bolus titrated to response.
Use paediatric observation charts. Trends matter more than single readings. Escalate early using PEWS or local tools.

cards.title: Section 2 Summary
cards.body: Key Learning Points

bullets.label: Hypotension may occur late in paediatric shock. Treat on early clinical signs — don't wait.
Treat airway and breathing changes urgently. Respiratory failure is the commonest route to paediatric arrest.
Always apply paediatric-specific emergency protocols. Weight-based dosing is non-negotiable.
Reassess response to every intervention. Document trends and escalate using structured communication tools.
This section supports your NCLEX preparation.
bullets.text: This section supports your NCLEX preparation. Review paediatric-specific normal ranges, emergency drug calculations, and escalation frameworks as part of your study plan.

cards.title: GNPS Programme 7: Paediatric Nursing
cards.body: Section 3: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care

cards.title: What This Section Covers
cards.body: Children with chronic or complex conditions rely on multiple medicines, devices and caregivers. Safe care demands precision, family education and seamless coordination across every setting.

bullets.label: Advanced weight-based dosing and infusion management
Long-term plans for complex paediatric diagnoses
Linking hospital, school and community services
Empowering families for safe discharge and home care

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Calculate weight-based doses, infusion rates and verify compatibility accurately
Deliver holistic care for children with chronic and multifaceted diagnoses
Collaborate with multidisciplinary teams and community providers
Ensure caregivers are confident, competent and equipped before going home

cards.title: Medication & Infusion Safety
cards.body: Paediatric dosing leaves no room for error. Every calculation must account for the child's current weight, concentration, infusion rate, drug compatibility and maximum permissible dose.

bullets.label: Technology supports — but never replaces —
bullets.text: Technology supports — but never replaces — independent double-checking by a registered nurse. Always verify manually before infusion commencement.

bullets.label: Children grow rapidly. Doses must be
bullets.text: Children grow rapidly. Doses must be recalculated whenever weight changes, particularly for neonates and infants on long-term regimens.

cards.title: Common Chronic Paediatric Conditions
cards.body: Long-term conditions require care plans that support not just clinical needs, but development, education and family life.

bullets.label: Inhaler technique, trigger avoidance and personalised action plans
Blood glucose monitoring, insulin administration and hypoglycaemia management
Seizure recognition, rescue medication and emergency action planning
Airway clearance, nutritional support and cardiac monitoring

cards.title: Coordinating Care Across Services
cards.body: Effective coordination ensures no child falls through the gaps. A clear care plan defines who does what, when and how across every setting.

bullets.label: School nurse, social worker, primary care GP
Responsibilities clearly documented and accessible to all

cards.title: Family Education: The Foundation of Safe Discharge
cards.body: Families are the primary caregivers at home. Their confidence and competence are non-negotiable before discharge.

bullets.label: Practical instruction on administration, storage and device use
When and how to seek urgent medical attention
Written, personalised plans for acute deterioration
Scheduled reviews with clear contact points for concerns

cards.title: Teach-Back & Return Demonstration
cards.body: Understanding cannot be assumed. Use structured techniques to confirm — not just deliver — learning before the family leaves the ward.

bullets.label: Both parents or all primary caregivers should demonstrate independently before discharge is confirmed.
"Can you tell me in your own words how you will give this medication at home?"
Ask the caregiver to physically demonstrate the skill — e.g. drawing up a rescue dose.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Epilepsy Discharge
cards.body: A child with epilepsy is being discharged with rescue medication. This scenario illustrates best practice across all core competencies.

bullets.label: Recalculate the rescue medication dose against the child's current weight — not the weight recorded at admission.
Provide clear, practical instruction to every primary caregiver, not just one parent.
A personalised emergency action plan that can be shared with school and community services.
Ask each caregiver to demonstrate administration independently before discharge is approved.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Consolidate your understanding of Section 3 with these essential principles for NCLEX preparation and clinical practice:

bullets.label: Whenever the child's weight changes — especially in neonates and infants
Across home, school, hospital and community with clear, shared responsibilities
Confirm understanding through return demonstration — with every caregiver
Provide clear, written action plans for all acute situations before discharge
NCLEX Tip: Questions on paediatric medication
bullets.text: NCLEX Tip: Questions on paediatric medication safety frequently test weight-based dosing, caregiver education and multidisciplinary coordination — all covered in this section.

cards.title: GNPS Programme 7: Paediatric Nursing
cards.body: Section 4: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care

cards.title: Setting the Scene
cards.body: Why This Section Matters

bullets.label: International paediatric nurses operate at the
bullets.text: International paediatric nurses operate at the intersection of children's rights, family dynamics and cultural diversity. This section equips you with the knowledge to:

bullets.label: Recognise and respond to safeguarding concerns
Communicate effectively across cultures and age groups
Navigate consent, assent and adolescent privacy
Apply trauma-informed principles in everyday care
Competence in these areas is essential for NCLEX preparation and safe international practice.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: What You Will Be Able to Do

bullets.label: Identify physical, emotional and behavioural indicators of abuse or neglect.
Use age-appropriate, culturally respectful communication with children and families.
Apply principles of legal consent, child assent and adolescent privacy correctly.
Use evidence-based strategies to minimise distress for vulnerable children.

cards.title: Safeguarding Responsibilities
cards.body: Safeguarding is a core legal and professional duty for every paediatric nurse — regardless of clinical setting or country of practice.

bullets.label: Unexplained bruising, burns, fractures or injuries inconsistent with the child's developmental stage.
Withdrawal, aggression, regression, fearfulness or changes in school performance.
Poor hygiene, malnourishment, inadequate clothing or missed medical appointments.
Always follow local legal and organisational pathways promptly. Delay in reporting can place the child at greater risk.

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Communication Access in Paediatric Care

bullets.label: Effective communication protects patient safety
bullets.text: Effective communication protects patient safety and builds trust. In paediatric care, this means adapting your approach for every family encounter.

bullets.label: Professional interpreters must be used for complex clinical discussions — never rely on family members
Children deserve honest, simple explanations suited to their age and cognitive ability
Cultural humility means asking, not assuming, about family communication preferences

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Consent, Assent and Adolescent Privacy

bullets.label: Paediatric consent involves multiple parties. Each requires a distinct nursing response.
Provided by parents or legal guardians. Required for all procedures and treatment decisions.
Involves the child in decisions appropriate to their maturity. Respects their developing autonomy.
Teenagers require confidential conversations within legal and safety boundaries.

cards.title: Trauma-Informed Care in Paediatrics
cards.body: Children who have experienced trauma require a predictable, safe and empowering clinical environment. Trauma-informed care is not a diagnosis — it is a universal approach.

bullets.label: Explain every step before it happens to reduce fear and build trust.
Give children small, safe choices to restore a sense of control.
Use a quiet tone, neutral body language and non-threatening positioning.
Avoid unnecessary physical restraint — explore comfort-based alternatives first.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario
cards.body: Putting It All Together: An Adolescent Disclosure

bullets.label: An adolescent requests a private conversation
bullets.text: An adolescent requests a private conversation with their nurse, raising concerns about medication management and home safety.

bullets.label: Honestly outline what can be kept private and when disclosure is required.
Create a safe space. Use open-ended questions and reflective listening.
When immediate risk is disclosed, activate the local safeguarding pathway promptly.

cards.title: NCLEX Readiness
cards.body: Key Learning Points for Exam and Practice

bullets.label: These four principles underpin safe,
bullets.text: These four principles underpin safe, rights-based paediatric nursing and are tested across NCLEX-RN scenarios involving children, families and culturally diverse populations.

cards.title: Section 4 Complete
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series · Programme 7

bullets.label: Recognise indicators and follow reporting pathways without delay.
Use professional interpreters and age-appropriate language always.
Involve children in decisions according to maturity and legal frameworks.
Prioritise predictability, choice and calm in every interaction.
Proceed to the next section or review your NCLEX practice questions on paediatric safeguarding and communication.
